title.source: Checking a claim before you share it

essentialQuestion.source: How can you find out if a story is true before you share it?
essentialQuestion.back: How can you know whether something is true before you share it?

learningGoal.source: Use lateral reading to check a made-up news story against other sources, explain why copies add no evidence, and decide whether to share it.
learningGoal.back: Use lateral reading to check a made-up news story against other sources, explain why copies do not add evidence, and decide whether to share.

read.sections.0.heading.source: Ask three questions before you share

read.sections.0.text.source: Messages can spread very quickly, and a shocking story often travels fastest. In Brightwater, a page called Brightwater Daily Truth posted that the town bridge would close for a whole year. It said, “Share this before they delete it.” Words like these push people to hurry, and hurrying makes it easy to share something false. Before you share, ask three questions. Who is behind the information? What is the evidence? What do other sources say? The Brightwater post gives no names, no evidence and no link to the town council, which looks after the bridge.
read.sections.0.text.back: Messages can spread very fast, and shocking stories often spread fastest. In Brightwater a page called Brightwater Daily Truth posted that the town's bridge would close for a whole year. The post said “Share before they delete it.” Words like these push people to hurry, and hurrying makes it easy to share untrue stories. Before sharing, ask three questions. Who is behind this information? What is the evidence? What do other sources say? The Brightwater post has no person's name, no evidence, and no link to the town council, which looks after the bridge.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: Messages spread fast. Shocking stories spread fastest. A page in Brightwater said the bridge would close for a year. read.sections.1.heading.back: Read across to other sources, like a fact-checker

read.sections.1.text.source: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people judge real websites about social issues. There were 10 historians who teach at universities, 10 professional fact-checkers from news organisations and 25 Stanford students. In one task, they compared the websites of two doctors' groups that gave advice about bullying. Most historians thought both sites were reliable. The fact-checkers quickly left each page and opened other sources to find out who was behind it. This is called lateral reading, which means reading sideways across many sources instead of down one page. The fact-checkers reached better answers in much less time. The researchers chose a small group on purpose, so the study shows how these experts worked, not how everyone reads.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 2017 researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people judge real websites about social issues: 10 historians who teach at universities, 10 professional fact-checkers from news organisations and 25 Stanford students. In one task they compared the websites of two groups of doctors that give advice about bullying. Most historians thought both websites were trustworthy. The fact-checkers quickly left each page and opened other sources to find out who was behind it. This way is called lateral reading, meaning reading across to many sources instead of reading down within one page. The fact-checkers got better answers in much less time. The researchers deliberately chose a small group, so this study shows how this group of experts works, not how everyone reads.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people check real websites. There were 10 historians who teach at universities. There were 10 fact-checkers and 25 students. In one task, they looked at two doctors' groups' websites about bullying. Most historians thought both sites were good. The fact-checkers left each page fast. They opened other sources to find out who made it. This is called lateral reading. It means reading sideways. The fact-checkers got better answers, faster. read.sections.1.simpler.back: In 2017 researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people check real websites. There were 10 historians who teach at universities, 10 fact-checkers and 25 students. In one task they looked at the websites of two groups of doctors about bullying. This way is called lateral reading, meaning reading across to other sources. The fact-checkers got better answers, faster. This group was small, so the study shows how this group of experts works, but not how everyone reads.

read.sections.2.text.source: Agreement helps only when sources have their own evidence. Several websites can repeat the same claim because they all copied one post, and ten copies are still only one source. The town council looks after the bridge, so it knows the dates: two days of repairs, not a whole year. The radio and the fact-checkers asked the council and say the same. The chat page only copied the first post word for word, so it adds no evidence. So the first post is false. Don't share it; share the council's notice instead. Sometimes you can't check a claim, for example with no internet. Then ask a teacher or wait. News can change, so check again later, for example if the repairs take longer.
read.sections.2.text.back: Sources agreeing helps only if each source has its own evidence. Many websites may repeat the same claim because they all copied one post, and ten copies are still one source. The town council looks after the bridge, so it knows the dates: two days of repairs, not a whole year. The radio and the fact-checkers asked the town council and said the same. The chat page just copied the first post word for word, so it adds no evidence. So the first post is not true. Do not share it; share the town council notice instead. Sometimes you cannot check a claim, for example when there is no internet. Then ask a teacher or wait. News can change, so check again later, for example if the repairs take longer.

watch.summary.source: This short video explains lateral reading. It is a way to check information that professional fact-checkers use. Many people check a website by reading down the page. They look at how it looks and what it says about itself. But a page can look serious and still give false or one-sided information. Fact-checkers do something different. After a quick look, they leave the page. They open new pages and search for what other sources say about it and about who is behind it. By reading less of the page and more about it, they learn more, and they learn it faster. You can do the same thing. Before you trust a page, find out who made it and what others say about it.
watch.summary.back: This short video explains lateral reading, a way of checking information that professional fact-checkers use. Many people check a website by reading down the page: they look at how it looks and what the site says about itself. But a web page can look serious and still give untrue or one-sided information. Fact-checkers do it differently. After a quick look they leave the page, open a new one and search for what other sources say about that page and the people behind it. By reading less on the page and more about the page, they learn more, faster. You can do the same: before trusting a web page, find out who made it and what others say about it.

educatorNotes.1.source: The research in section 2 is Wineburg and McGrew (Stanford History Education Group working paper, 2017; a shortened version in Teachers College Record, 2018–19). The 45 participants, chosen on purpose rather than at random, were 10 PhD historians teaching at universities in California and Washington, 10 professional fact-checkers at news and fact-checking organisations and 25 Stanford undergraduates. They judged live websites and searched the web on social and political issues: for example, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the much smaller American College of Pediatricians on bullying (most historians thought both reliable; most students rated the second more reliable), and who paid for a teacher-tenure lawsuit. The authors note the small samples and timed tasks. The group became the independent Digital Inquiry Group in January 2024.
educatorNotes.1.back: The study in part 2 is Wineburg and McGrew (Stanford History Education Group working paper 2017, and a shorter version in Teachers College Record 2018–19). The 45 participants were chosen purposively, not at random: 10 PhD historians teaching at universities in California and Washington, 10 professional fact-checkers at news and fact-checking organisations, and 25 Stanford undergraduates. They judged real websites and searched the internet on social and political issues, such as the American Academy of Pediatrics versus the much smaller American College of Pediatricians on bullying (most historians thought both trustworthy; most students rated the second more trustworthy) and who paid for a lawsuit about teacher tenure. The authors note the sample was small and the tasks were timed. The group became the independent Digital Inquiry Group in January 2024.
educatorNotes.1.note: "teacher-tenure lawsuit" as คดีฟ้องร้องเรื่องสิทธิการจ้างงานถาวรของครู; the two American organisations keep their English names. Reviewer: Stanford in Latin letters, as elsewhere in the course.

educatorNotes.2.source: Lateral reading normally needs the internet. On an offline device the activity's source cards stand in for new pages, and the print view lists them for work on paper; a teacher can also play “the other sources”. The evidence shows only the post, so learners meet the other sources in the activity. Write and Speak use what the learner found there rather than repeat the check. In Indonesia, Mafindo recommends fact-checking sites such as TurnBackHoax and CekFakta (Liputan6, 2026).
educatorNotes.2.back: Lateral reading usually needs the internet. On devices without internet the activity's source cards can stand in for new pages, and the print page lists these cards for paper use. Teachers can also play “the other source” themselves. The evidence shows only the post, so learners find the other sources in the activity. The Write and Speak steps use what learners found in the activity rather than asking them to check again. In Indonesia, Mafindo recommends fact-checking sites such as TurnBackHoax and CekFakta (Liputan6, 2026).
